catalog_citation: Wilhelmsen, Vera. 2018. A Linguistic Description of Mbugwe with Focus on Tone and Verbal Morphology. Studia Linguistica Upsaliensia 20. Uppsala: Acta Universitatis Upsaliensis (PhD diss., Uppsala University). 262 pp. urn:nbn:se:uu:diva-347793.
catalog_locator: Abstract (unnumbered, p.4); sec. 2.4 Summary p.60; sec. 3.2.1 'Phonemic tone and TBU' pp.65-66; sec. 3.2.2.1 p.68; fn.26 p.74.
catalog_quote: [Abstract] Mbugwe has two tones, high and low, and the low tone is considered the default tone. The tone-bearing unit is the mora. High tones spread one mora to the right, and the last high tone before a low tone is upstepped. There is both lexical tone and grammatical tone in Mbugwe, and grammatical tones that occur on the verb stem in certain verb forms are described. [p.60] Tone is of course part of the phonology of Mbugwe, and will be treated in chapter 3. [p.65] As this section will show, Mbugwe is analysed as having only one tone specified underlyingly, that is the H tone. The surface L tones are assumed to be a result of “Default L-insertion,” which occurs fairly late in the phonology ... Each TBU is either H or L in noun roots, but the lexical tonal distinction is found only in the first syllable of the verb root. [p.66] Only vowels carry tone in Mbugwe. [p.68] However, several of the ØHØ nouns are loans from Swahili, and they tend to take a H tone on the penultimate syllable, since Swahili has penultimate stress. [p.74 fn.26] The last vowel is also lengthened and devoiced towards the end. This is a phonetic effect that always happens to an utterance-final toneless vowel, and it is not marked in the transcription.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mbugwe is described purely as a tone language (underlying H vs toneless, mora as TBU, rightward H spread, upstep, final lowering); the 261-page description contains no statement on word stress or accent placement. The only prosodic prominence facts given are tonal, plus the remark that Swahili loanwords carry an H on the penult mirroring Swahili penultimate stress, and phonetic lengthening/devoicing of an utterance-final toneless vowel (not penultimate lengthening).
new_statements.exceptions: Swahili loans (CVCVCV nouns) tend to have H on the penultimate syllable, attributed to Swahili penultimate stress (p.68).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone described on words in isolation (nouns elicited in isolation, whistled) and in utterances; final lowering and final-vowel lengthening are utterance-level. No word-level stress domain is defined because no stress is described.
new_statements.identity_note: Wilhelmsen's data are from Magugu at the southern end of the Mbugwe area (fieldwork 2011-2012) plus the SIL FLEx database; language-level Mbugwe [mbug1242], iso mgz, self-name Buwe. Not to be confused with Mbugu/Ma'a [mbug1240] (Mous 2003), which has a separate folder in this compilation.

sources.note: Nothing about word stress in Mbugwe itself. Ch.2 Phonology (pp.40-60) and ch.3 Tone (pp.61-99) analyse Mbugwe as tonal: one underlying tone (H) vs toneless, mora = TBU, H tone spread one mora rightward, upstep, final lowering. The only occurrences of 'stress' are p.68 (Swahili loans 'tend to take a H tone on the penultimate syllable, since Swahili has penultimate stress') and two non-prosodic uses. fn.26 p.74: an utterance-final toneless vowel is phonetically lengthened and devoiced.
